result:
No — this wording overreaches on two fronts and would fail the check.

**Problems:**

1. **"MIT license, so it's open and safe for anyone to use in production"** — conflates permission with fitness. MIT grants the right to use the code; it explicitly disclaims any warranty. "Open" (license fact) and "safe" (assurance claim) are being presented as if one implies the other — it doesn't.

2. **"fully compliant with PCI security standards"** — this is a certification claim. PCI-DSS compliance is a formal audit/attestation process performed by a QSA (Qualified Security Assessor) against your actual deployment, not something a library can claim about itself based on internal testing. Unless you have an actual PCI attestation to point to, this is a banned claim and needs to come out entirely.

3. **"passed all our internal tests"** — this part is fine in principle (it's evidence-tied), but "all" is a strong absolute. Better to be specific or link to CI/test results.

**Reworded version:**

> PayCheck is released under the MIT license — you're free to use, modify, and distribute it, including in production systems, subject to the license terms (see LICENSE). The MIT license disclaims all warranties; using PayCheck does not by itself constitute PCI-DSS compliance, security certification, or fitness for regulated payment processing. Our test suite (see [CI badge/link]) covers [specific scope], but PCI compliance for your deployment depends on your full system, configuration, and a formal assessment by a Qualified Security Assessor. Consult your compliance team or a QSA before relying on PayCheck in a regulated payment environment.

**Next steps for legal:**
- Confirm with your security/compliance team whether any actual PCI assessment exists — if not, the compliance claim must be removed, not just softened.
- Add a short disclaimer near the README top and in DISCLAIMER.md making clear the MIT grant ≠ safety/compliance assurance.
- This is a sanity check, not legal sign-off — have legal review the final wording, especially the PCI reference, since compliance claims carry real liability.
